articles.title: Free and Open Indo-Pacific: A Pillar of Deeper Regional Cooperation
articles.excerpt: In July 2026, the foreign ministers of the Quad countries — Japan, the United States, Australia, and India — met on the sidelines of the ASEAN Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in Manila and issued the “Joint Press Release on Quad Cooperation with ASEAN,” reaffirming their support for ASEAN centrality and unity and the “ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific (AOIP).” The Quad foreign ministers also reaffirmed their commitment to a “Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP)” and outlined their intention to deepen cooperation with ASEAN, with FOIP as a core pillar. It has been ten years since former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe proposed the FOIP at the Sixth Tokyo International Conference on African Development (TICAD VI) in Nairobi, Kenya, in August 2016. Abe viewed Asia and Africa, and the Pacific and Indian Oceans, as an inseparable and integrated region, and expressed Japan’s determination to maintain “freedom from coercion,” the “rule of law,” and a “market economy” across it. The FOIP philosophy won broad acceptance across the Indo-Pacific, from advanced Western nations such as the United States and Australia to developing countries including African nations, India, and ASEAN member states. In June 2019, ASEAN adopted the AOIP as its own Indo-Pacific vision, guided by principles including ASEAN centrality, inclusiveness, and respect for international law. In promoting FOIP, Japan has placed particular emphasis on cooperation with ASEAN. Southeast Asia is a strategically vital region connecting the Pacific and Indian Oceans, and one facing pressure to change the status quo by force or coercion. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi attended the Japan-ASEAN Summit in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, in October 2025. At the meeting, she stated Japan’s commitment to safeguarding the peace, stability, and prosperity of the Indo-Pacific together with ASEAN, by evolving FOIP — a core pillar of Japanese diplomacy — and deepening synergy with the AOIP.

articles.title: A Message to China from Japan’s Takaichi Administration
articles.excerpt: The Taiwan Strait came up as an example during a debate on the legal applications of Japan’s right of collective self-defense at the Budget Committee of the Lower House on November 7, 2025, and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi gave her response when asked under what circumstances a “survival-threatening situation” would be legally applicable. China reacted sharply, to say the least: verbally accusing Japan of “neo-militarism” and then moving to normalize activities by the Chinese Navy — especially its aircraft carriers — in the waters between the First Island Chain and the Second Island Chain, while its coast guard began deploying east of Taiwan’s coast. On the economic front, security provisions were applied to Japanese companies, restrictions were imposed on rare earth exports, and measures were taken to curtail tourism and other exchanges with Japan, with economic, local-governmental, and academic ties all affected to a significant degree. China has demanded that Takaichi retract her November 7 statements, but she has refused. An APEC summit is scheduled in China in November 2026, hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Takaichi is expected to attend. Significant progress in Japan-China relations has been elusive, however. A Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson made remarks in late June 2026 that appeared to give the green light for private exchanges between Japan and China, and a range of business associations and parliamentary groups are now scheduled to visit China this fall. Whether this supposed “green light” actually came from China’s leadership remains unclear. So what message is the Takaichi administration sending to China? First, on the Taiwan Strait. Three days after the original remarks, at a Budget Committee session on November 11, 2025, Takaichi said that “Peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait are important not only for Japanese security but also for the stability of the international community as a whole.

articles.title: Humanoid Robots and China’s Vision of the Future
articles.excerpt: The robots lined up on the track. For a moment, it looked almost like an ordinary athletics meet. Then the race started. The machines lurched forward, their metal legs struggling to keep their balance as they sprinted toward the finish line. One of them, a Chinese humanoid robot called Tiangong Ultra, finished the 100 meters in 8.64 seconds – faster than Usain Bolt’s human world record. The scene took place this August at the World Humanoid Robot Games in Beijing, where more than 2,000 robots competed in 51 events. Some ran and boxed. Others performed household chores or industrial tasks. Some simply fell over. It was part sporting event, part technology demonstration, and part vision of the future. And the way that future was described was revealing. In Western coverage, the event was often framed as a spectacle, a demonstration of Chinese state power or even propaganda. Chinese state media had a different emphasis. The focus was less on the event itself and more on what the robots might eventually do: work in factories, move through warehouses, assist in homes or become part of everyday life. Neither interpretation is necessarily wrong. Beijing clearly wants to showcase China’s technological progress, and the World Humanoid Robot Games was designed to do exactly that. But the difference in emphasis is striking. The same robots can be seen as a technological achievement, an industrial strategy, or a piece of political theater. Reducing the event to the latter risks missing what is happening on the technological side. China’s humanoid robotics industry is not simply a governmental display. The country has invested heavily in the sector, and Chinese companies are developing robots for factories, logistics, healthcare, and other commercial applications. The Robot Games are part of that broader strategy. They are designed not only to show what robots can do, but also to test how they might be used outside the laboratory. That does not make the games any less political.

articles.title: Public Scrutiny Really Does Help the Unjustly Detained
articles.excerpt: Every August 30, the international community observes the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances. Historically, any mention of enforced disappearances has evoked images of clandestine detentions and unacknowledged abductions by shadowy operatives operating with impunity in totalitarian states. In the contemporary era, however, the architecture of erasure has evolved into something far more institutionalized. Across authoritarian regimes and even democracies, state apparatuses frequently achieve the same outcome through formal legal machinery: weaponizing extraordinary counterterror statutes in the name of national security, imposing endless pre-trial detention, and relying on procedural delays to remove dissenting voices from the public sphere. Nowhere is this tension between extraordinary security legislation and constitutional safeguards more evident than in India’s handling of civil society advocates exposing the most serious human rights violations. As we speak, a film dedicated to the life of Jaswant Singh Khalra – who exposed enforced disappearances in Punjab in the 1990s and who himself became a victim of enforced disappearance – has been banned by the Indian government. Notably, the case of Kashmiri human rights defender Khurram Parvez illustrates how thin the line between public witness and administrative oblivion has become. For over two decades, Parvez dedicated his life to documenting human rights violations and unearthing the records of enforced disappearances in Jammu and Kashmir. In an unsettling paradox, the advocate who spent his career ensuring that the vanished were not forgotten has become the target of institutional silencing himself. Arrested in November 2021 by the National Investigation Agency under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA), Parvez has spent nearly four-and-a-half years in pre-trial incarceration without the commencement of a substantive trial.

articles.title: Nepal’s Floods Upset Its China-India Balancing Act
articles.excerpt: Nepal’s recent floods, which have killed at least 1,280 people while over 5,600 are still missing as of this writing, rank among the country’s worst natural disasters. Preliminary estimates put economic losses at $2.56 billion. But the disaster’s consequences will extend far beyond the immediate human and economic toll. It has also undermined the efforts of successive post-2015 governments to achieve more geopolitical balance, largely through the development of new transport, trade and transit facilities with China. As a landlocked country wedged between India and China, Nepal has long sought to preserve its strategic autonomy by balancing the influence of its two neighbors. For a variety of reasons, India, which surrounds the country on three sides, has blockaded its open border with Nepal three times since 1969 — most recently in 2015. That year, Nepal promulgated a new constitution that had failed to address India’s concerns. At other times, New Delhi has openly meddled in Nepali politics. To reduce that vulnerability to Indian pressure, Nepali rulers have felt the need to increase engagement with China, the northern neighbor. After the 2015 blockade, the then-K.P. Sharma Oli government signed a slew of agreements with China to establish new trade and transit links. As part of the process, a significant investment was made to upgrade the Kerung border point (known as Gyirong on the Chinese side) into an all-weather international crossing. Much of China-Nepal trade has gradually shifted to Kerung from Tatopani, the previous main artery of bilateral trade that was badly damaged by the 2015 earthquakes. Unfortunately, the recent floods literally washed away much of the investment around Kerung. There is not even a trace of the customs buildings and customs yards — on either side of the border. After the flooding of the Kerung border, China has also shut down Tatopani, citing possible landslides on the Nepali side.

articles.title: Indonesia’s Emerging China Dependencies
articles.excerpt: As ASEAN’s only G20 member, a critical global mineral supply chain node, and occupying strategic maritime space, massive Indonesia is an especially consequential “fulcrum of order” in the Indo-Pacific and Global South. Like most ASEAN states, it remains committed to strategic autonomy while notably drifting toward China. However, Jakarta’s shift is especially consequential. “Free and active,” or bebas aktif, remains Indonesian foreign policy’s sincerely prized core. Yet beneath this high-level continuity, Beijing’s influence has rapidly grown, especially economically, overtaking the United States and key alternative partners like Japan and South Korea. Indonesia is not yet China-aligned, but the material bases for a “free and active” foreign policy are eroding. Jakarta’s preferred orientation requires not just intent but robust options. China’s role within Indonesia’s economy may become so indispensable and entrenched that Jakarta cannot meaningfully tell Beijing no, hollowing out free-and-active rhetoric. Indonesia’s high-priority, ambitious growth goals and mixed economic picture sharpen this dilemma. Given its strategic importance, a functionally China-aligned Indonesia would have profound regional consequences. Indonesia’s Distinct China Shift Within Southeast Asia, Indonesia’s China shift is distinct. The Anatomy of Choice Alignment Index shows that among major ASEAN states – Indonesia, Vietnam, Singapore, Philippines, Malaysia, Thailand – Jakarta moved furthest toward China relative to the United States from 1995 to 2024. The shift was overwhelmingly economically driven, with inbound investment flows decisively shifting in Beijing’s favor. Lowy’s Southeast Asia Influence Index adds Japan, South Korea, and Australia to the picture. With the possible exception of Malaysia, Indonesia’s overall and economic balance of influence is the most tilted toward China.

articles.title: Why Australian Politics Is Shifting Right, Not Left
articles.excerpt: The reasons for the rise of far-right politics in Australia are often cited as financial stress, housing shortages, and frustration with the government. Yet this doesn’t explain why disillusioned voters are drifting toward the far right instead of the left. To understand this, we need to look at how far-right ideas actually connect to mainstream Australian values – not treat the far right as some separate, foreign, or imported movement. The common assumption is that far-right politics is fundamentally opposed to democratic values, or is a kind of “sickness” in an otherwise healthy system. But Cas Mudde argued the opposite: “The radical right isn’t a rejection of mainstream values, it’s an extreme version of them.” This means that the drift to the right has grown out of ideas already normal and accepted, just pushed further. To see this, it helps to look at the three core ingredients of far-right politics – nationalism, authoritarianism, and populism – and ask how much of each already exist in Australian life. Nationalist language is nothing new in Australian politics. Phrases like the “national interest,” “Australian values,” and warnings about the “nation in danger” are everywhere, and people who disagree with those phrases are often branded “un-Australian.” This has deep roots. The dispossession of and violence against First Nations peoples was foundational to the Australian state, and Irene Watson argued that this violence remains built into Australian law today. One of the very first laws passed by the new Federal Parliament in 1901 was the White Australia Policy, which tied national identity directly to race. We like to think we’ve moved past this. But in the lead-up to the 2016 election, then-Immigration Minister Peter Dutton claimed refugees “won’t be numerate or literate” and would be “taking Australian jobs.” These two claims, that refugees are simultaneously incapable and a threat, are not as contradictory as they sound.

articles.title: The Real Key to the AI Race: Nanometers or Gigawatts?
articles.excerpt: For years, the race for artificial intelligence leadership has been framed as a contest over advanced semiconductors. But the decisive advantage may belong not to the country that manufactures the best chips, but to the one that can deploy the most computing power across its economy. In the AI era, nanometers still matter. Yet increasingly, so do gigawatts. China’s emerging strategy, including plans to connect AI data centers via a national computing network and expand supporting energy infrastructure, reflects a broader belief that AI leadership will be determined by large-scale deployment. Governments focusing mainly on semiconductor fabrication may be chasing past advantages instead of future ones. China’s reported plan to invest roughly 2 trillion yuan (i.e., $295 billion) over five years in a nationwide network of interconnected AI data centers underscores the scale of this strategic shift. We can compare the global data center expansion trajectory. For the United States, McKinsey’s latest analysis puts U.S. data-center power capacity at 30-plus GW in 2025, rising to 90-plus GW by 2030. For China, Rystad estimates China’s total data-center capacity will rise from 32 GW at the end of 2025 to more than 60 GW in 2030. AI facilities are expected to increase from 39 percent of capacity in 2026 to 48 percent in 2030, implying roughly 29 GW by 2030. In the same study, it was estimated that global capacity would reach 155 GW, meaning the United States and China combined would account for roughly 77 percent of global AI capacity. The computing landscape has evolved, with smaller transistors giving countries with advanced fabrication technologies a competitive edge. The U.S. and allies have traditionally led in semiconductor manufacturing, while China is increasing its own capabilities to reduce reliance on foreign technology.

articles.title: In Cambodia, Floating Houses Are Stuck Aground as Climate Change Takes Hold
articles.excerpt: Siem Reap province, Cambodia — A 63-year-old woman watched her two grandchildren play on dry ground beneath her high-stilted house in mid-July. By this time of the year, Pou village in Siem Reap province is normally flooded as the nearby Tonle Sap lake rises and expands with the monsoon. Stilted houses would be perched over the water, while floating houses drift on the bloated river. When Sok Rina was young, the water would begin rising in June, flooding the riverbank and surrounding forests by July. The floodwaters would become rich with fish, supporting the livelihoods of villages on the water. Recently, however, the Tonle Sap has been low, year after year. Researchers are seeing a change in Cambodian weather patterns as climate change takes hold across the world. The traditional monsoon season in June and July appears to be weakening, even as intense easterly storms return in September and October. At the same time as weather patterns are changing, more than 200 large dams are planned, completed, or under construction in the lower Mekong basin. Together, climate change and hydropower dams are restricting the flow of water into the Tonle Sap. And without water, there’s no fish. In Siem Reap province, residents of Pou, Me Chrey and Chong Khneas villages say they are facing severe challenges to their survival. Collapsing Fisheries Cheim Oeurn, 40, caught only about one kilogram of fish one July morning. It was all small climbing perch and moonlight gourami, which have almost no market value. The Sangkae river is too low for fish to spawn in the flooded forests around Tonle Sap, he said. Rising water temperatures in shallow areas also threaten to destroy fish eggs. “If there is a lot of water, there will be more fish; as the water rises, fish will breed. Less water means fewer fish,” Cheim Oeurn said. In the past, fishers in Pou village could earn 50,000 to 100,000 riel ($12.50 to $25) daily with a 50- to 60-kilogram catch.

articles.title: How the Chinese Government Has Controlled the Narrative on the Tibet Floods
articles.excerpt: As rescue efforts have continued on both sides of the border following the devastating floods in Nepal and Tibet, a fight over how the disaster is being reported has been growing in intensity on social media. The dispute centers on the claims and counterclaims following a story by the BBC’s China correspondent, Laura Bicker, about how China is censoring videos of the floods. Bicker said videos of the landslide and flood surge sweeping through Gyirong Port on the border was scrubbed from the internet, in part, because Beijing fears instability in the politically sensitive region of Tibet. Some social media users, however, have posted screenshots of the footage used by the BBC, pointing out it had actually been shown in the Chinese media. One Chinese journalist put it bluntly: “Never seen the BBC spread rumors so blatantly.” Another X user said the “middle ground often gets lost” in heated debates like this over Chinese censorship. The Chinese government has long complained about what it sees as Western media “bias” in reporting on Tibet. Its supporters seem to have doubled down on this narrative this week on social media, zeroing in on the BBC. But Chinese social media users, both inside and outside China, have long dealt with the authorities exercising control over information. This has certainly been the case in the aftermath of the floods, too. As Bicker noted in her report, the most concrete example is the deletion of videos showing the massive wave of mud and water swallowing Gyirong Port. The footage was initially circulated on the platforms Weixin and RedNote, but users later could not access it. Another form of control has been the restricted access for independent and foreign journalists. Allyson Horn of the Australian Broadcasting Corporation said she had made repeated requests to travel to Tibet, but was denied. Other foreign journalists have similarly been blocked.

articles.title: Human Rights Are Essential to Australia’s Interests
articles.excerpt: World politics feels like it is in disarray. Rules intended to regulate the behavior of all countries and institutions seem not to matter. International human rights norms now appear decidedly unfashionable, even in Australia, a country that should be one of the staunchest defenders of global human rights, where I have just spent two weeks meeting with government officials and civil society. Transactional power politics increasingly disregard internationally agreed rules, enabling powerful governments, from China and Russia to the United States and their allies, to accelerate violations of human rights with few consequences. But the longing for human rights is not going away. Respecting them remains critical for so many people around the world, especially those facing the most severe repression. In recent years, protesters throughout Asia – often led by young people – have fought for rights and equality in Bangladesh, Nepal, Sri Lanka, and India, even at the cost of their lives. Democracies that remain committed to human rights and a rules-based world order should recognize that. Instead of cowering to this geopolitical moment, they should seize the uncertainty by doubling down and recognizing that rights are central to their long-term national interests. Canberra should be first in line. Instead, Australia and other democracies have become focused on military security, diminishing the focus on human rights. In the past year, Australia has prioritized signing new regional defense and security agreements while doing little to re-energize a rules-based world order. To be sure, military and cyber threats pose real dangers in this new world disorder. But coercion from abroad can take many forms. It also works by intimidating exiled dissidents, silencing journalists, corrupting democratic institutions, and exporting surveillance. Defense pacts alone cannot address these tactics.

articles.title: US Unpredictability Is Giving Its Asian Allies New Reasons to Cooperate
articles.excerpt: When U.S. President Donald Trump abruptly ordered the Pentagon to substantially reduce joint military exercises with South Korea, officials in Seoul were caught off guard. The annual Ulchi Freedom Shield drills still went ahead, but were cut short on Trump’s order. The episode was a reminder that even one of Washington’s closest allies can find the assumptions of its security policy changed with little warning. That uncertainty is why, across the Indo-Pacific, several of the United States’ closest partners are investing more heavily in relationships with one another – and, increasingly, with Europe. South Korea and Japan are expanding cooperation on supply chains, energy and advanced industries. Japan and Australia are linking economic security more closely to defense production and military operations. All three are also building more structured ties with the European Union. Of course, these efforts are not an attempt to replace the United States. China’s growing power, North Korea’s weapons programs, Russia’s war in Ukraine, and repeated disruptions to energy and supply chains were already pushing like-minded countries closer together. But Trump’s second term has added another incentive: the need for relationships that remain useful when U.S. policy changes suddenly, including toward its own allies. South Korea and Japan offer the most politically unlikely example. Their relationship has repeatedly been derailed by disputes over Japan’s colonial rule, wartime labor and historical memory. The rapprochement begun under former South Korean President Yoon Suk-yeol and former Japanese Prime Minister Kishida Fumio therefore looked vulnerable to political turnover. Instead, it has continued under progressive President Lee Jae-myung and conservative Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae. In his August 15 Liberation Day address, Lee pointed to a year of shuttle diplomacy with Japan and highlighted cooperation in supply chains, energy, and advanced industries.

articles.title: Cockroach Jolt Opens Up Opposition Space for Mocking Modi
articles.excerpt: No great movement designed to change the world (or a nation) can bear being laughed at or belittled, argued Czech-French novelist Milan Kundera in his 1967 novel, “The Joke.” “Mockery is a rust that corrodes all it touches,” he wrote. In the summer of 2026, a satirical protest movement calling itself the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) — a wry play on India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) — did something few observers thought possible in Narendra Modi’s India: it made mockery of the prime minister feel normal. The movement was born out of the mockery of a remark by the chief justice of India and quickly resonated with youth anger over recruitment and examination controversies. Examination paper leaks became a rallying point. Demonstrators adopted the cockroach as their emblem — a creature that has survived fumigation, starvation, and every known odds. During agitations in the national capital, young protestors carried posters with caricatures of Modi, performed skits mimicking Modi’s mannerisms, and chanted slogans laced with profanity directed at the prime minister. Videos of these performances spread rapidly across Instagram, X and WhatsApp. Modi has been ruling the country with tight control since 2014. His government does not respond well to dissent and criticism. Satirists and stand-up comedians have had an increasingly tough time in Modi’s India. Cracking jokes at ruling party politicians, or anything even obliquely related to the Hindu faith and practices, can lead to court cases or mob violence. Kundera’s larger insight was that authoritarian structures rely on total obedience, absolute gravity, and a carefully manufactured image of infallibility. Jokes, satire and parodies of state propaganda weaken the regime’s psychological control. But once the powerful become objects of collective laughter, their aura of inevitability can begin to crack. In India, July 2026 unleashed waves of mockery.

articles.title: Australia Should Work With China, Not Try to Contain It
articles.excerpt: Greg Sheridan has always been provocative. The foreign editor of The Australian is well known for his strident view that Australia should fully embrace American military power. One recent sermon focused on the need to support the U.S. Navy base at HMAS Stirling. “Frankly,” he writes, “I’d much rather entrust Australia’s security to the U.S. Navy than to the Albanese government.” Sheridan then moves to flattery for Labor’s resident Kentucky Colonel, aka the minister for AUKUS, Richard Marles. Marles, he says, has “done quite well on the critical question of U.S. alliance management.” Despite his distaste for most things Labor, Sheridan concludes that Marles is a good fit for the job at hand: kowtowing to the U.S. military and its boss, the belligerent Pete Hegseth. He claims we don’t need to pretend that Stirling is an Australian military base because “we actively and happily shelter under the U.S. extended nuclear umbrella.” Sheridan proposes that the U.S. and Australia should now draw up “common battle plans” to prepare for conflict with “the only candidate for adversary – China” There is no doubt China has developed its People’s Liberation Army (PLA) land, navy, air force, marines, rocket force, and cyber warfare capabilities to now claim military ascendancy in the South China Sea and beyond. In June, the Lowy Institute in Sydney released a well-researched analysis of the PLA’s military strength entitled “Understanding the Chinese military threat to Australia.” Authored by Sam Roggeveen and David Vallance, the study is good work. It explains China’s rise and President Xi Jinping’s aim to complete China’s “great rejuvenation” by 2049, the 100th anniversary of Mao’s revolutionary victory. By then, the authors assert, China will be a prosperous, technologically advanced and a global military superpower – “a world class force.” Many would say this has already been achieved.

articles.title: Securing Navigation for Trans-Caspian Trade
articles.excerpt: Until March 2026, the primary threats to developing trade corridors across the Caspian Sea seemed to be inadequate infrastructure and falling water levels. Then Israel targeted Iranian naval assets in the sea, followed in July by a Ukrainian attack on Iranian military shipments in the waterway. Conflict in the Caspian Sea has made it clear that physical maritime security is essential to making the east-west route a viable, reliable alternative conduit for critical resources. The Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, the east-west route known as the Middle Corridor, provides 4,250 kilometers of rail lines and 500 kilometers of sea connections between Europe and Central Asia, transiting through Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan. The Middle Corridor will also potentially connect further to China via a new rail line through Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan and link Armenia and Azerbaijan through the 42-kilometer Zangezur Corridor thanks to the U.S.-sponsored TRIPP deal. A second route, the International North-South Transport Corridor, once developed, would span 7,200 kilometers and connect Russia to the Persian Gulf, via the Caucasus, the Caspian Sea, and India. Conceived more than 20 years ago, the proposed north-south route has gained new life due to Russia’s need for alternative routes since the full-scale war in Ukraine and India’s interest in a route to the Arctic circumventing China. Both trade routes highlight the Caspian region’s centrality for supply chain resilience and the expansion of connectivity. Nevertheless, many bottlenecks prevent these ambitions from reaching fruition. The World Bank argues that trade along the route could triple by 2030 if ten priority actions are taken immediately. These include improving port infrastructure and rail connections, increasing the quantity of rolling stock, and addressing customs, logistics, and governance challenges. The declining water level of the Caspian Sea exacerbates these challenges.

articles.title: Vietnam Sentences 11 to Death in Country’s Largest Ever Drug Trafficking Case
articles.excerpt: A Vietnamese court yesterday sentenced 11 people to death and 19 to life imprisonment in one of the country’s largest ever drug trafficking cases. The case dates back to March 2023, when four flight attendants for Vietnam Airlines were ‌caught carrying narcotics hidden in toothpaste tubes at Ho Chi Minh City’s Tan Son Nhat International Airport, after arriving on Flight VN10 from Paris. The tubes contained more than 2.9 kilograms of ketamine and 8.3 kilograms of MDMA. The Ho Chi Minh City People’s Court yesterday sentenced 11 people to death for illegal drug trafficking in connection with the case. This included the alleged ringleader Ha Danh Nam, 52, from Nghe An province, who remains on the run and is one of four defendants being tried in absentia. All 11 were also fined between 50 and 100 million dong ($1,916 and $3,832) each. Prosecutors allege that Nam “organized the transportation of drugs from France to Vietnam by air and through international express delivery services,” disguised as consumer goods from France into Vietnam, according to the state media outlet VnExpress. They said that drugs “were concealed in toothpaste, dietary supplements, confectionery, and other consumer goods.” Members of the network then used delivery services, encrypted messaging platforms such as Signal and Telegram, and bank accounts registered under other people’s names in order to distribute the drugs throughout Vietnam while evading detection. Among the 19 defendants who received life terms was Hoang Sy Thang, 39, and his nephew-in-law Bui Van Anh, both also from Nghe An, who ran the network’s main storage point and were convicted of the illegal transport of narcotics.

articles.title: Japan’s FOIP 3.0: Is Pragmatism That Delivers Resilience Enough?
articles.excerpt: Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae meets with Vietnam’s President and Communist Party chief To Lam, in Hanoi, Vietnam, May. 2, 2026. Credit: X/MOFA of Japan When Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae visited Vietnam in early May this year, she presented an “evolved version” of the Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP), a key plank in Japanese foreign policy, which is being called FOIP 3.0. The “Updated FOIP” specifies as priority areas “Building economic infrastructure for the age of AI and data,” “Co-creation of economic growth opportunities through public-private collaboration and rule sharing,” and “Enhancing cooperation in the field of security to ensure regional peace and stability,” each with its own items for concrete cooperation. The FOIP was first proposed by the late Prime Minister Abe Shinzo in a speech in Nairobi in 2016. The keyword for FOIP 1.0 was “connectivity,” reflecting the fact that it was launched in the middle of a major shift in the power balance triggered by the rise of China. International division has only deepened since, following the outbreak of the Russo-Ukrainian war, and with the rise of the Global South, international politics have become more complex still. It was in response to this that then Prime Minister Kishida Fumio proposed the New Plan for a FOIP, or FOIP 2.0, in 2023, along with the keyword “inclusiveness.” Building on this foundation, the keyword for FOIP 3.0 as proposed by the Takaichi administration is “resilience.” With any improvement of relations with China unlikely in the near time, and with the United States pursuing an exceedingly unpredictable foreign policy under Trump, Japan faces what might be called a double risk. It needs to deepen cooperation with Indo-Pacific countries to mitigate those risks and ensure autonomy and resilience.

articles.title: Escaping the Escalation Trap in the Thailand-Cambodia Maritime Dispute
articles.excerpt: The Gulf of Thailand forms the second axis of the Cambodia-Thai border dispute. The 27,000-square-kilometer Overlapping Claims Area has been disputed since 1972 and is estimated to hold some 1.6 billion barrels of oil and 17 trillion cubic feet of natural gas. Thailand terminated the 2001 memorandum of understanding governing talks over the OCA in early 2026, after fighting along the two nations’ disputed land border in July and December 2025. The outbreak of war reignited historic territorial and political animosities between the two Southeast Asian states and resulted in a border closure that still persists. The immediate cause of the fighting was a calculated political leak by Cambodian Senate President Hun Sen of a private 17-minute telephone conversation with Thai Prime Minister Paetongtarn Shinawatra. The recording exposed Paetongtarn adopting a deferential posture toward Phnom Penh while offering critical remarks regarding her own military commanders. As Hun Sen no doubt intended, the political fallout in Bangkok was swift. The leak locked Thai political elites into a severe audience cost escalation trap, where public outrage severely restricted their diplomatic flexibility. Paetongtarn’s political credibility evaporated almost overnight, and a wave of hyper-nationalism culminated in her suspension and removal from office by the Constitutional Court. Domestic political discourse in Thailand became thoroughly militarized, effectively ending any immediate possibility of bilateral compromise with Cambodia. Riding this surge of populist anger, Anutin Charnvirakul and his Bhumjaithai Party secured victory in the February 2026 election. Anutin formed a hardline government that explicitly prioritized security, deferring border management directly to military commanders. Fulfilling a key electoral pledge to his nationalist base, Anutin’s cabinet formally approved the unilateral termination of the 2001 MoU.

articles.title: Indonesia’s President Pitches His Country as Russia’s ‘Gateway’ to Southeast Asia
articles.excerpt: Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto yesterday described his country as Russia’s gateway to Southeast Asia, as he pushed for closer trade and investment ties between the two nations. Speaking at the Eastern Economic Forum (EEF) in Vladivostok alongside Russian President Vladimir Putin, Prabowo urged Russian businesses to invest in Indonesia, stating that the Pacific should become a “highway between our two economies.” “For Eurasian businesses, Indonesia is a natural entry point to ASEAN,” Prabowo said, according to a report by the Straits Times. He described the two nations as having ” very profound and important historical ties that have lasted for more than five decades” and said that Moscow was “an important partner” for Jakarta. Prabowo apologized to Putin for having skipped the ASEAN-Russia Commemorative Summit in Kazan in June, which was attended by leaders from 10 of ASEAN’s 11 member states, and joked that he was paying off my ‘debt’ now by coming to Vladivostok.” Prabowo also extended an invitation for Putin to visit Indonesia at some point in the future. In his own address at the EEF, which was established in 2015 with the aim of drawing investment into the underdeveloped Russian Far East, Putin emphasized the importance of Russia’s relationship with Asia in general and Indonesia in particular. He said that the Asia-Pacific “is a powerful centre of growth and sets the pace for the development of the entire global economy.” “Russia is an active participant in investment and trade cooperation in the Asia-Pacific region,” he added. “We interact as equals with our partners and with the region’s leading integration groupings.” Putin also told Prabowo that he regarded Indonesia as “one of Russia’s trusted friends in ASEAN.” Prabowo was the EFF’s main guest of honor, a year after he was accorded the same privilege at the St Petersburg International Economic Forum.

articles.title: The Japan-Thailand Relationship: Light and Shadow
articles.excerpt: The relationship between Japan and Thailand is closer than ever. Interdependence across economics, security, and human exchange has deepened, bringing shared benefits and opportunities alongside new challenges in the form of supply chain vulnerabilities and transnational crime. Understanding the Japan-Thailand relationship today requires a clear view of both its “light” and its “shadow.” Diplomatic relations between Japan and Thailand date to the 1887 declaration of friendship (officially, the Declaration of Amity and Commerce Between Japan and Siam), with the 140th anniversary falling in 2027. The two countries have built a close relationship grounded in a long history of exchanges and warm ties between their imperial and royal families. Economic ties deepened dramatically after World War II, and in recent years cooperation has extended to shaping international trade rules, as evidenced by Japan’s support for Thailand’s OECD accession. At the Japan-Thailand Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in June 2026, Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi and his Thai counterpart Sihasak Phuangketkeow confirmed that the two countries would enhance their Comprehensive and Strategic Partnership and deepen cooperation under the Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP) initiative. Light: Creating Rules in an Unstable Economic Order Thailand is one of Japan’s biggest manufacturing hubs in Southeast Asia and a key investment destination. Foreign investment in Thailand (on an approved-investment basis) rose by about 68 percent year on year in the first half of 2026, with Japan among the top investors alongside Singapore and China. As U.S. protectionism disrupts the international economic order, maintaining free and fair trade rules has become a shared challenge for Japan and Thailand. Emblematic of this is Japanese support for Thailand to join the OECD (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development).

articles.title: The Climate Crisis Is Stretching the Nepali Military Beyond Its Limits
articles.excerpt: The footage of the avalanche that triggered devastating floods along Nepal’s Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers near the China-Nepal border on August 26 is deeply sobering. The road, bridges, customs, and immigration office with China, and the entire settlement and traditional bazaar along the riverbank, were wiped out in a moment. In the wake of the flood, the Nepali government deployed security forces, including the Nepal Army, Nepal Police, and Armed Police Force, as first responders. Nepal has put more than 20,000 security personal into responding to the disaster, possibly the largest such deployment since the aftermath of the 2015 earthquake. The collapse of local and provincial governments and the inaccessibility of flood-affected areas prompted the government to rely on the security forces at a desperate moment. The use of security forces in disaster response is not new in Nepal. Security forces often get involved, ranging from rescue and relief operations to rehabilitation activities. The Nepali Constitution 2015 (2072 BS) enshrined a provision for deploying the military in national crises arising from disasters and development projects. The National Security Policy (2016) also considers climate change and the environment as part of the national interest. But the ad hoc stretching of the security forces into disaster response can result in the security forces themselves being increasingly exposed to vulnerabilities and capacity constraints amid the climate crisis in Nepal. As environmental disasters become more frequent and severe in the Himalayan region, the recent flood must be an important case study in the growing complexity of the military’s engagement in disaster governance and preparedness. The scale and intensity of the recent flood was unimaginable and it is becoming evident that there were significant casualties among security forces.

articles.title: Australia’s Broken Hill: Where Children Are Sacrificed to Mining Interests
articles.excerpt: Broken Hill is an Australian mining town steeped in history. The town’s legacy of union struggles for workers’ rights is chronicled through street plaques, protected heritage buildings, and murals reminiscent of early-20th-century Mexican muralism. Under the expansive grey sky over Broken Hill, enormous mining wealth has been created – stretching from Australia to northern Chile and further. As with most forms of wealth, it is rooted in human hardship. In Broken Hill, mining wealth has been accumulated at the cost of children’s exposure to lead contamination. Last July, Australia’s New South Wales (NSW) state government, which includes Broken Hill, announced AU$37.3 million (approximately US$26.74 million) to address lead contamination. The funding, as stated in the announcement, will lead to a “twofold increase in the number of homes remediated annually, including the removal of lead-based paint to eliminate lead contamination, the installation of grass to trap dust, and enhanced monitoring of emissions from existing mines and other localized dust sources.” In Broken Hill, emissions from mining and smelting are the primary source of exposure. Elevated blood lead levels among local children signal a public health crisis. The announcement “underscored a commitment to protect children and families from the long-term effects of lead exposure.” The funding announcement follows a January 2026 report on reducing the health and environmental impacts of lead contamination in Broken Hill. The NSW Office of the Chief Scientist & Engineer (OCSE) issued the report. “A long history of lead mining in Broken Hill has left a legacy of widespread contamination and human exposure,” said Professor Hugh Durrant-Whyte, OCSE’s NSW Chief Scientist, in the report. “While some progress has been made in reducing environmental lead levels and community exposure, improvements have slowed in recent years,” he added.

articles.title: Ezra Jin Is Free, But There Are More Pastors in China Behind Bars
articles.excerpt: This July, a miracle took place in China, when Ezra Jin, an imprisoned Christian pastor from an unregistered house church, was suddenly set free. Throughout his 266 days of imprisonment, the international community rallied behind Pastor Jin, culminating in his release. I write this article in desperate need of one more miracle. My father, Pastor Gao Quanfu of the Light of Zion Church, and my mother, Pang Yu, remain behind bars. My father faces 12 to 13 years in prison on baseless charges of fraud. As their trials approach, I can only hope that the international community will similarly support their cause. For my parents, faith and service were a calling. My father became a Christian at age 28, at a time when public religious practice was nearly nonexistent in China. He served as a minister for 40 years: mentoring the next generation of religious leaders, carrying out ministry work, and supporting families in his congregation. He was also a talented musician; he played an instrument called the suona horn. My mother had a successful career as an actress, TV anchor, and producer. It was love at first sight for the two of them, and they anticipated a bright future for their family and community. In 2025, my parents paid a steep price for their faith. On May 16, authorities in Xi’an arrested Pastor Gao and eleven other members of the Light of Zion Church. Initially, my father was charged with “using superstition to undermine the implementation of the law.” The charges were later altered; he is now facing charges of “fraud” for accepting voluntary donations from his congregants. Three weeks after my father’s arrest, my mother was detained, simply because she is married to Pastor Gao. My parents’ ordeal is reflective of a wider crackdown on unregistered house churches in China.

articles.title: The Meaning Behind Pakistan’s First Lunar Rover
articles.excerpt: The lunar South Pole has emerged as a major focus of international space exploration due to its scientific potential. In view of this, Pakistan has also decided to send its own scientific mission there. The country’s first indigenous lunar rover, Jinnah 1, will head to the Moon’s South Pole in 2029 aboard China’s Chang’e 8 mission. Pakistan’s decision to undertake a lunar mission reflects three key perspectives. First, the gesture is symbolic as Islamabad also wants to be among the group of elite member countries conducting scientific research on the Moon, indicating its growing interest in the space sector. Second, the mission signals the revival of an old rivalry on the Moon, as India reached the lunar South Pole with Chandrayaan 3 in 2023. Lastly, Jinnah 1 illustrates increasing cooperation between Pakistan and China in the space domain. Jinnah 1 aims to explore and study the geological characteristics of the lunar surface and conduct key experiments for future lunar research. The rover is likely to weigh around 35 kg and have an expected price tag of approximately 400 million rupees ($1.4 million). It will have a panoramic camera, ground-penetrating radar, and a device to analyze minerals in lunar soil using infrared spectroscopy. It will also be equipped with a device for taking soil samples, analyzing and separating the noble gases contained therein, and storing them. Before analyzing why Pakistan decided to send its own lunar mission, it is equally important to understand why different states are sending their own expeditions to the Moon’s South Pole. The region is believed to be suitable for long-term human habitation due to its vast, untapped ice reserves. If the surface contains large quantities of ice, it can be used not only to produce hydrogen fuel for deep-space propulsion but also to provide drinking water for humans residing there. This will exponentially reduce costs for future lunar and interplanetary explorations.

articles.title: US Allies in Asia Are Paying for the Iran Stalemate
articles.excerpt: While the United States still has military options available against Iran, these are unlikely to isolate Tehran from its allies. Despite a new round of sanctions, the regime remains defiant. The key issue for the current administration is that it lacks the willingness to confront China and Russia over their assistance to the regime, and is instead urging Beijing’s cooperation as it looks ahead to Donald Trump and Xi Jinping’s meeting on September 24. Under the current stalemate, Washington’s allies in Asia are disproportionately affected, at a time where they are being asked to take on a greater share of the regional deterrence burden. Both China and Russia continue to materially aid Iran and are alleged to have provided intelligence assistance that helped it strike American bases across the region. China has provided drone components, navigation modules, chemical precursors for missile propellant, shoulder-fired systems, and continues its purchases of discounted Iranian crude. Russia has supplied upgraded drones built off Iran’s own design from its Alabuga factory in Tatarstan, along with satellite imagery and damage assessments enabling strikes on American assets. The entities involved have been sanctioned, yet they have adapted. Washington has designated Chinese companies, sanctioned tankers and warned banks against dealing with the refineries in Shandong province that import and process Iranian crude. Beijing responded by shifting to overland routes through Pakistan and Central Asia, and by issuing a blocking order that exposes any company obeying the American sanctions to Chinese penalties for doing so. Both Washington and Beijing have pulled their punches, proving they value their trading relationship more than they do the outcome of the Iran war. After the October 2025 summit, an American export control rule covering the subsidiaries of blacklisted firms was suspended, and China lifted its export controls on critical minerals.

articles.title: Central Asia’s Energy Transition Depends on Water Security
articles.excerpt: Central Asia is building a new energy system. Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan are rapidly expanding solar and wind generation and battery storage, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan are expanding their hydropower capacity, and governments across the region are investing in stronger cross-border electricity connections. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are also both moving ahead with nuclear power. These projects are usually discussed as separate parts of the region’s energy transition, but they are increasingly connected by single, critical variable: water. Climate change is making Central Asia’s hydrology less predictable just as electricity demand is growing. Drought can constrain hydropower, extreme heat can increase power demand, irrigation systems consume large amounts of electricity, and new generation assets must be able to operate for decades under water conditions that may look very different from historical averages. This creates a challenge, but also an opportunity. A more integrated and flexible Central Asian power system could reduce not only the cost of the energy transition, but also the region’s exposure to water shocks. Five Energy Systems, One Regional Opportunity Central Asia does not have a single energy model. Kazakhstan remains strongly dependent on thermal and coal-fired generation. Uzbekistan’s system is still largely gas-based, although solar, wind, and battery storage are expanding rapidly. Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan rely heavily on hydropower, while Turkmenistan relies predominantly on natural gas. These differences are often treated as vulnerabilities, but they can also create complementarity. Hydropower and reservoirs can provide flexibility to systems with growing shares of variable renewable energy. Solar and wind can reduce dependence on hydrological conditions. Thermal generation can provide firm capacity while storage expands.

articles.title: Security Is the Key to Resolving the Thai-Cambodia Border Conflict
articles.excerpt: With UNCLOS conciliation proceedings between Thailand and Cambodia now formally under way, Thailand is preparing to engage constructively. We would have preferred to resolve the matter directly with Cambodia. Direct diplomacy is usually faster, less cumbersome and, when there is sufficient political will, more effective. But Thailand is a State Party to UNCLOS, the U.N. Convention on the Law of the Sea. We accepted the process and will take part in good faith, with the interests of the Thai people and our sovereign rights firmly in view. That willingness to engage through international law should not be mistaken for a willingness to treat every dispute along the Thailand-Cambodia border as if it existed in a vacuum. They do not. A boundary is not drawn on a blank sheet of paper. It is surveyed on actual ground, by actual people, in communities that need to be safe enough for technical work to take place. This is the point that risks being lost in Cambodia’s push to convene the Joint Boundary Commission, because no technical or legal process can be separated from conditions on the ground. Before survey teams can do their work, the border must be sufficiently safe, stable, and properly managed. That means implementing the commitments already agreed by both sides on ceasefire and de-escalation, joint demining, and cooperation against transnational crime. These measures are what make credible border discussions possible in the first place. Consider demining. Thai soldiers have repeatedly been injured by landmines along the border, including incidents involving mines that have been identified as newly laid. Just a couple weeks ago, yet another Thai deminer lost a limb. Whatever political narrative one prefers, a mine does not become less dangerous because a meeting has been scheduled. Nor can a Joint Boundary Commission survey team be expected to work in an area potentially littered with mines. Joint demining is a practical prerequisite to constructive talks.

articles.title: K-Beauty’s Brazil Push Signals a New Type of Korean Diplomacy
articles.excerpt: The Koreas | Diplomacy | East Asia As strange as it sounds, the Korean beauty industry is playing an increasingly important role in Seoul’s foreign policy calculus. K-Beauty products on display at a store in Almaty, Kazakhstan. Credit: Shutterstock During a state visit to Brazil in late July 2026, South Korean President Lee Jae-myung called for a deeper partnership between Brazil and South Korea built on the following three pillars: commercial aircraft, critical minerals, and K-Beauty. While the first two are familiar agenda items across modern strategic partnerships, the third is decidedly not. Cosmetics rarely share space with jet manufacturing and rare earths, and their place on Lee’s diplomatic agenda reveals a lot about the Korean beauty industry’s growing role in Seoul’s foreign policy calculus. Lee’s comment came at a Korea-Brazil business roundtable in São Paulo on July 28, where alongside delegations from companies like Samsung and HD Hyundai, the CEOs of K-Beauty titans AmorePacific Holdings, APR, Goodai Global, and Silicon2 joined the trade delegation. Meanwhile, a separate two-day showcase titled “K-Beauty Glow Big in Brazil” ran alongside the summit to put beauty brands like Beauty of Joseon, d’Alba, Isntree, and Mixsoon before Brazilian retail buyers. Alongside the presidential roundtable, a second official channel was unfolding over the same period. On July 27, First Vice Minister Roh Yong-seok of the Ministry of SMEs and Startups met Brazil’s cosmetics association ABIHPEC and the e-commerce giant Mercado Libre, where they agreed to pursue joint research and marketing that pairs Amazon’s natural ingredients with South Korean cosmetic technology. According to Roh, such a partnership could pave the way for cosmetics becoming “the world’s number one export item,” provided the industry keeps strengthening and diversifying its markets. For all of this forward-looking ambition, K-Beauty’s entanglement with geopolitics is nothing new.

articles.title: ‘We Are Horrified’: Academic Freedom at Risk With Uzbek Professor’s Arrest in Kazakhstan
articles.excerpt: In late August, BBC Uzbek broke the news that an Uzbek professor working in Kazakhstan had been arrested nearly two months prior on allegations of espionage. Very little is known about the case of Dr. Ikboljon Qoraboyev, a 46-year-old international relations professor at Maksut Narikbayev University in Astana, originally from Andijan, Uzbekistan. Questions from the BBC Uzbek and other media outlets to both Kazakh and Uzbek authorities have yielded silence in answer. When Vlast, an independent Kazakh media outlet, asked Maksut Narikbayev University (MNU) about Qoraboyev, the university distanced itself from the professor, stating that he “is not currently a professor at the university. For any further information concerning his detention, please refer to the relevant competent authorities.” According to the initial BBC Uzbek report, and additional reporting by RFE/RL’s Kazakh Service, Azattyq, on July 3, people in civilian clothes took Qoraboyev from his home in Astana where he lived with his wife and three children. A relative who spoke to BBC Uzbek said they were told he was being charged with espionage under Article 176 of Kazakhstan’s Criminal Code. Article 176 defines espionage as the collection, theft or storage of “state secrets” by a foreign national for the purpose of transfer to a foreign state, or an international or foreign organization “for use against the national interests of the Republic of Kazakhstan.” Conviction carries a prison sentence of 10 to 15 years. BBC Uzbek reported that Qoraboyev’s most recent research focused on critical minerals in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, noting he’d produced a paper in April titled “Comparative legal, political and strategic narratives around important minerals in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.” Colleagues told BBC Uzbek that work was based on publicly available information. The paper has not yet been published.

articles.title: Mohan Malik on Trump, Asia, and the Legacy of the Global War on Terror
articles.excerpt: Beyond the Mekong | Security | Southeast Asia The veteran strategist and security analyst joins Beyond The Mekong to discuss the region’s ongoing security challenges. President Donald J. Trump attends the Memphis Safe Task Force roundtable on public safety at the Tennessee Air National Guard Base, Tennessee, on Monday, March 23, 2026. Credit: Official White House photo by Molly Riley Mohan Malik is a veteran China-Asia analyst and military strategist who has advised senior brass on geopolitics at the U.S. Defense Department’s Asia-Pacific Center for Security Studies and is a former director of Defence Studies at Deakin University in Australia. Malik spoke with The Diplomat’s Luke Hunt, his former student, about how China, Asia, and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) are shaping up as U.S. President Donald Trump prepares for the mid-term elections and as the world marks 25 years since the 9/11 attacks that spawned the Global War on Terror. Also known as the 9/11 Wars, the Global War on Terror ended with the withdrawal of U.S.-led forces from Afghanistan five years ago. Left behind was a vastly different geopolitical landscape, whose ramifications have continued to influence diplomacy in China, Asia, and ASEAN to this day. ASEAN is divided between maritime and mainland countries but also by religion, mainly Buddhism, Christianity, and Islam, and Malik says they are still confronted by major problems. But some nations emerged from the 9/11 Wars stronger than others. “Thailand, Indonesia, and India in South Asia, to some extent Sri Lanka to Bangladesh have done relatively better, they have been able to manage, contain the threat of domestic terrorism,” he said. China also emerged in a stronger position and is now facing headwinds from the Trump administration and perhaps ASEAN, which wants to finalize its Code of Conduct in the South China Sea with Beijing by the end of this year.

articles.title: Landtagswahl Sachsen-Anhalt: Linke erobert drei Direktmandate, der Rest geht an die AfD
articles.excerpt: Die rechtsextreme AfD holt bei der Wahl in Sachsen-Anhalt wohl 38 von 41 Direktmandaten. Bei der Wahl 2021 hatte sie eins, der Rest ging damals an die CDU. Allein die Linke konnte nun auch mit Direktkandidaten punkten. 06.09.2026, 22.57 Uhr Linken-Spitzenkandidatin Eva von Angern auf der Wahlparty der Linken Foto: Katharina Kausche / dpa Das amtliche Endergebnis steht noch aus, aber schon jetzt zeichnet sich ab, dass die AfD einen Großteil der 41 Direktmandate in Sachsen-Anhalt gewonnen hat. Bei der vergangenen Landtagswahl im Jahr 2021 gingen noch 40 der 41 Direktmandate an die CDU – und nur eines an die AfD. Dieses Mal geht kein Direktmandat an die Christdemokraten, dafür aber offenbar 38 der 41 Wahlkreise an die rechtsextreme AfD. Das zeigt der bisherige Auszählungsstand. Der amtierende Ministerpräsident Sven Schulze (CDU) unterliegt in seinem Wahlkreis Magdeburg III wohl dem AfD-Politiker Christian Mertens. AfD-Spitzenkandidat Ulrich Siegmund siegt dagegen in seinem Wahlkreis Genthin mit mehr als 50 Prozent. Allein der Linken gelingt es, in drei Wahlkreisen den Durchmarsch der AfD zu stoppen: Mustafa Groener siegt in Magdeburg II, Gitta Hartenstein-Wiermann in Halle II, und Jannik-Loris Balint holt ein Direktmandat in Halle III. Im Karl-Liebknecht-Haus freut man sich über den Minierfolg. Er sei das Ergebnis ehrlicher Handarbeit, sagte Linkenchefin Ines Schwerdtner dem SPIEGEL. »Die Linke kann als glaubhafte, soziale und antifaschistische Kraft direkt gegen die AfD gewinnen.« Es sei gelungen, »rote Leuchttürme zu bauen«. Mehr zum Thema 1 Min 3 Min 3 Min Dass die Linke ausgerechnet in den beiden größten Städten des Bundeslandes punkten konnte, ist stimmig. Die Partei hat sich am deutlichsten als antifaschistisch positioniert, baute auf eine junge, weibliche Zielgruppe, queere und migrantische Menschen. Kurz: Die Linke punktete im urbanen Milieu.

articles.title: Viernheim in Hessen: Tote und Verletzte bei Absturz von Kleinflugzeug über Hessen

articles.title: Florida: Amazon-Frachtflugzeug rammt bei Landung mehrere Fahrzeuge – mindestens fünf Tote
articles.excerpt: Ein Frachtflugzeug des Amazon-Konzerns ist am US-Flughafen Miami verunglückt. Nach Angaben der örtlichen Feuerwehr rollte die Maschine über die Landebahn hinaus, rammte mehrere Fahrzeuge und fing Feuer. Der Prime Air Frachter war vom Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan auf der Karibikinsel Puerto Rico gestartet, wie die US-Luftfahrtbehörde auf der Plattform X mitteilt. Empfohlener externer Inhalt An dieser Stelle finden Sie einen externen Inhalt von X.com, der den Artikel ergänzt und von der Redaktion empfohlen wird. Sie können Ihre Zustimmung jederzeit wieder zurücknehmen. Externen Inhalt anzeigen Ich bin damit einverstanden, dass mir externe Inhalte angezeigt werden. Damit können personenbezogene Daten an Drittplattformen übermittelt werden. Mehr dazu in unserer Datenschutzerklärung. Bei dem Vorfall sind mindestens fünf Menschen ums Leben gekommen. Fünf weitere seien verletzt ins Krankenhaus gebracht worden, erklärten Behördenvertreter und die Polizei auf einer Pressekonferenz. Zunächst gab es keine genaueren Informationen zu den Todesopfern – damit blieb unklar, ob Besatzungsmitglieder des Flugzeugs oder Menschen am Boden betroffen waren.Die Maschine kam neben oder auf einer Straße zum Stehen, da sind die Angaben und Aufnahme von vor Ort nicht eindeutig. Nach Angaben der Feuerwehr ereignete sich das Unglück am frühen Nachmittag (Ortszeit). Auf Videos war zu sehen, wie Rauch aus einer Boeing 767 aufstieg. Wie es zu dem Unfall kam, ist bislang unklar. Die US-Luftfahrtbehörde hat Ermittlungen aufgenommen. Flugverkehr wurde zwischenzeitlich eingestelltEine Amazon-Sprecherin schrieb auf der Plattform X, beim Landeversuch habe es einen Zwischenfall gegeben. Man arbeite eng mit den Behörden zusammen, um zu verstehen, was genau passiert sei. Amazon hat eine eigene Frachtfluggesellschaft, um Pakete schneller über lange Distanzen zu transportieren. Ob das Flugzeug beladen war, blieb unklar. Der Flug erfolgte laut Amazon über eine Partnerairline.

articles.title: Wahlsieg in Sachsen-Anhalt: AfD hofft auf das große Chaos
articles.excerpt: Die AfD will ihren Wahlerfolg als den Beginn eines Durchmarschs verstanden wissen. Zwar verfehlt sie wohl die absolute Mehrheit. Doch ihrem strategischen Ziel – der Zerstörung der CDU – kommt sie ein gutes Stück näher.

articles.title: Sachsen-Anhalt: Internationale Pressestimmen zur Landtagswahl
articles.excerpt: Das starke Abschneiden der AfD und der herbe Absturz der CDU bei der Landtagswahl in Sachsen-Anhalt finden auch im Ausland viel Beachtung. Medien wie die BBC und die englischsprachige Seite des arabischen Senders Al Jazeera pushten die ersten Prognosen auf die Handys ihrer Leserinnen und Leser. Auf mehreren Onlineseiten war die Berichterstattung weit oben. USA»New York Times«: »Nach ersten Prognosen vom Sonntag dürfte die Partei ›Alternative für Deutschland‹ bei der Landtagswahl in Sachsen-Anhalt im Osten Deutschlands auf den ersten Platz kommen, was die Möglichkeit eröffnet, dass die extreme Rechte zum ersten Mal seit dem Ende der Nazizeit in einem Teil des Landes die Macht übernehmen könnte. … Dieser Zuwachs ging fast ausschließlich zulasten der Christdemokraten, der Partei von Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz, die heute Abend gemessen am Stimmenanteil mit Abstand die größten Verlierer sind.« Großbritannien»The Telegraph«: »Migrantenfeindliche AfD steuert in Ostdeutschland auf überwältigenden Wahlsieg zu.«BBC: »Seit dem Zweiten Weltkrieg hat in Deutschland noch nie eine Rechts-außen-Partei die Kontrolle über ein Bundesland übernommen. Eine Regierungsbeteiligung auf Landesebene würde Zuständigkeiten für die Polizei sowie für das Bildungs- und Kulturwesen mit sich bringen.«»Financial Times«: »Prognosen zufolge wird die Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) bei der Landtagswahl in Sachsen-Anhalt stärkste Kraft. Dies wäre ein Durchbruch für die Partei der äußersten Rechten und zugleich ein schwerer Rückschlag bei den Wahlen für die etablierten politischen Parteien Deutschlands.« »The Times«: »Sollten sich die Hochrechnungen bestätigen, wäre das Ergebnis eine persönliche Demütigung für Friedrich Merz, dem geraten worden war, den Wahlkampf fast gänzlich zu meiden – aus Angst, seine persönliche Unbeliebtheit könnte der AfD Auftrieb geben.

articles.title: Berlin: Hacker-Gruppe Rhysida veröffentlicht weiteres Datenpaket aus Leak
articles.excerpt: Ein weiteres Datenpaket aus dem groß angelegten Hackerangriff auf die Berliner Senatsverwaltung ist in der Nacht zum Sonntag veröffentlicht worden. Das teilte der Senat am Sonntag in der Bundeshauptstadt mit.Die nach der ersten Veröffentlichung gestohlener Informationen am Freitag ergriffenen Maßnahmen seien vorsorglich nochmals »in einigen Aspekten nachgeschärft« worden. Die zusätzlichen Maßnahmen könnten bei der Nutzung von Fachverfahren in der Bauverwaltung kurzfristig zu Einschränkungen führen, so die Senatskanzlei. »Alle Nutzerinnen und Nutzer werden darüber informiert«, so die Senatskanzlei. Auswirkungen seien auch für Bürgerinnen und Bürger möglich, sagte eine Senatssprecherin auf dpa-Anfrage. Dazu, um welche Fachverfahren es geht und um welche konkreten Maßnahmen, machte sie keine Angaben. Ein Fachverfahren ist etwa das Beantragen und Bewilligen von Wohngeld.Die kriminelle Hackergruppe Rhysida hatte sich vom 7. bis zum 12. August unbemerkt Zugang zu Teilen des Berliner Landesnetzes verschafft und Daten abgeschöpft. Betroffen waren die Senatsverwaltungen für Bauen und Verkehr. Die Verwaltung bemerkte den Angriff am 14. August und machte ihn drei Tage später öffentlich. Die Hacker wollten zwei Millionen Euro Lösegeld in Bitcoin erpressen, die Summe sollte bis Freitag gezahlt werden. Die Berliner Landesregierung erklärte aber, dass sie sich nicht erpressen lasse, und zahlte nicht. Nach Ablauf der Frist am Freitag wurden rund 1,4 Millionen Dateien zum Download angeboten.

articles.title: Robert Pattinson wird Vater eines Mädchens. Und hat plötzlich mehr Zeit für die Arbeit
articles.excerpt: Die Geburt seines Kindes hat Robert Pattinson laut eigenen Worten geholfen, sein hohes Arbeitspensum zu managen. In kurzer Zeit drehte der 40-Jährige die Filme »The Drama«, »Die Odyssee«, »Primetime« und den dritten Teil von »Dune«. Aktuell steht er für die Fortsetzung von »Batman« vor der Kamera. Pattinson und seine Partnerin Suki Waterhouse sind 2024 Eltern eines Mädchens geworden. »Zum ersten Mal in meinem Leben wusste ich etwa zwei Jahre lang, wie mein Zeitplan aussehen würde«, sagte der britische Filmstar in Venedig.Bei den Filmfestspielen präsentiert der Brite seinen Film »Primetime« von Lance Oppenheim. Waterhouse begleitete ihn auf dem roten Teppich. Das Baby habe ihm eher geholfen, sich auf die Arbeit zu fokussieren, als es ihn davon abgehalten hätte, so Pattinson. »Ich hatte keine Lust, abends auszugehen. Plötzlich hatte ich also doppelt so viel Zeit für alles Mögliche, was sehr, sehr hilfreich ist«, sagte er gegenüber der Nachrichtenagentur dpa.

articles.title: Donald Trumps Friedensplan: Muslimische Staaten verurteilen Israels Umsiedlungsplan für Gazastreifen
articles.excerpt: Die Außenminister acht muslimischer und arabischer Ländern haben gemeinsam die Pläne der israelischen Regierung für eine Umsiedlung der Palästinenser aus dem Gazastreifen verurteilt. Saudi-Arabien, Ägypten, Jordanien, die Vereinigten Arabischen Emirate, Katar, Pakistan, Indonesien und die Türkei erklärten, sie verurteilten »in schärfster Form« die von Israel »vorgeschlagenen Pläne und Mechanismen«, mit denen »Palästinenser mit Gewalt aus ihrem Land vertrieben werden« sollten. Der israelische Verteidigungsminister Israel Katz hatte am Mittwoch gesagt, Israel habe Pläne zur Umsiedlung von Palästinensern aus dem Gazastreifen. Die USA müssten allerdings noch klären, wohin die Bewohner umgesiedelt werden könnten.Einen Tag später sagte der rechtsextreme Minister für Nationale Sicherheit, Itamar Ben-Gvir, der Plan sehe im ersten Jahr die Umsiedlung von 250.000 Palästinensern aus dem Gazastreifen vor, die verbliebenen rund zwei Millionen Bewohner würden in den darauffolgenden sechs Jahren folgen. Mehr zum Thema 2 Min Auch Bundesentwicklungsministerin Reem Alabali-Radovan (SPD) hat den Plan als »inakzeptabel und menschenverachtend« kritisiert. »Wer davon redet, Menschen gegen ihren Willen umzusiedeln, spricht in Wahrheit von Vertreibung«, erklärte sie am Freitag. Der Plan stehe »im Widerspruch zum Völkerrecht«.Trumps Friedensplan in GefahrDie Außenminister der muslimischen Staaten warnten vor »schweren Konsequenzen«, wenn »Rufe nach Zwangsvertreibungen in erklärte Politik oder praktische Maßnahmen überführt werden«. Derartige Schritte stellten internationale Bemühungen um Frieden »direkt infrage«, besonders den Plan von US-Präsident Donald Trump zur Beendigung des Konflikts im Gazastreifen, »der eine strikte Ablehnung von Zwangsvertreibungen enthält«, fügten sie mit Blick auf den von Trump vorangetriebenen Gaza-Friedensplan hinzu.

articles.title: Thüringen.Gerecht: Frühere BSW-Mitglieder gründen nach Austritt neue Partei
articles.excerpt: Zwei Tage nach ihrem Austritt aus dem Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW) haben sich ehemalige Mitglieder in Thüringen zu einer neuen Partei zusammengeschlossen. Zur Vorsitzenden wurde die ehemalige BSW-Landeschefin und Finanzministerin Katja Wolf gewählt, wie Gründungsmitglieder in Erfurt mitteilten. Die Gründung am Sonntag kam sogar für Mitglieder der bisherigen Führungsmannschaft überraschend. »Es gab eine spontane Parteigründung«, hieß es. Die Partei nennt sich Thüringen.Gerecht. »Wir haben versprochen, für Stabilität und Verlässlichkeit in Thüringen zu sorgen. Jetzt laden wir alle Menschen ein, dieses Versprechen gemeinsam mit uns in die Tat umzusetzen«, erklärte Wolf laut einer Mitteilung. Der Gründungsvorstand werde so schnell wie möglich einen Gründungsparteitag einberufen, ergänzte die frisch gewählte Vorsitzende der neuen Partei.Thüringen.Gerecht stellt Kernthemen vorDie Gründungsmitglieder beschlossen demnach auch ein Gründungsprogramm mit sechs Kernthemen, die Thüringen.Gerecht künftig in den Mittelpunkt stellen will. Die neue Partei stehe für »gerecht bezahlte Arbeit, die Anerkennung ostdeutscher Lebensleistungen, industrielle Wertschöpfung und Innovation, eine intakte Umwelt, bezahlbare Energie, nachhaltige Investitionen und echte Bürgerbeteiligung«, hieß es in einer Mitteilung.

articles.title: Niederlande: Ronald Koeman Jr. trifft doppelt als Torwart in der Eredivisie
articles.excerpt: Torwart-Irrsinn in den Niederlanden: Der gleichnamige Sohn von Fußball-Ikone Ronald Koeman hat beim wilden 2:2 (0:0) von Telstar Velsen gegen Cambuur Leeuwarden in der Eredivisie einen Doppelpack vom Elfmeterpunkt erzielt. Nachdem Ronald Koeman Jr. in der 63. Minute per Strafstoß zum 1:2 verkürzte, behielt er in der elften Minute der Nachspielzeit ein weiteres Mal die Nerven und rettete seinem Club in Unterzahl einen Zähler. Der 31-Jährige lief nach seinem zweiten Treffer jubelnd auf die Fans zu, um die dramatische Wende zu feiern. »Ich bin natürlich sehr glücklich«, sagte Koeman bei ESPN. »Ich kann einfach gute Elfmeter schießen und habe das Selbstvertrauen, daher gibt es keine Zweifel.« Vor dem zweiten Strafstoß hatte der Torwart trotzdem noch einmal tief durchgeatmet – aus Gründen.Koeman Jr.: »Mich macht man nicht verrückt«»Du weißt, wie das läuft. Sie versuchen, auf dich einzureden. Aber mich macht man nicht verrückt. Eben einen Moment bei dir selbst sein und fokussieren«, erklärte Koeman. »Es ist schön, dass ich die Verantwortung übernommen habe. Es war die gleiche Ecke, vielleicht muss ich das in Zukunft etwas verändern. Aber wenn der Schuss hart ist, können sie ihn nicht halten.«

articles.title: Sachsen-Anhalt Wahl: Präsident des Zentralrats der Juden entsetzt über AfD-Wahlergebnis
articles.excerpt: Die Holocaustüberlebende Charlotte Knobloch hat sich erschüttert über das Wahlergebnis in Sachsen-Anhalt gezeigt. »An Tagen wie diesen fällt es mir schwer, meine Heimat noch wiederzuerkennen«, sagte die Präsidentin der Israelitischen Kultusgemeinde München und Oberbayern. »Dass Rechtsextreme in Deutschland in dieser Art wieder Wahlen gewinnen, das hätte ich mir in meinen schlimmsten Albträumen nicht vorstellen können.«Knobloch zufolge ist das hohe Wahlergebnis der AfD ein Zeichen, dass »die Statik der Demokratie in unserem Land nicht mehr funktioniert – und ich sage ganz offen: Das macht mir Angst.« Ein »erschreckend großer Teil der Wähler in Sachsen-Anhalt« habe die Grundlage von Demokratie, Sicherheit und Wohlstand abgelehnt. Damit hätten sie auch die Prinzipien zurückgewiesen, die es Juden und Jüdinnen ermöglichten, Deutschland wieder als ihr Zuhause zu begreifen. »Das ist ein tiefer Einschnitt – ganz egal, welche Partei am Ende den Regierungschef stellt.« Demokratische Parteien und Wähler müssten sich nun umso mehr für Freiheit, Respekt und Toleranz einsetzen, sagte Knobloch. »Wir dürfen – und ich will – dieses Land nicht verloren geben.«Josef Schuster sieht Gefahr für BildungspolitikDer Präsident des Zentralrats der Juden sprach von einem Resultat, das ihn »persönlich entsetzt«: »Über die letzten Monate war klar ersichtlich, welche Ziele die AfD verfolgt«, sagte Josef Schuster der »Welt«. »Wer sie heute gewählt hat – trotz oder wegen dieser Ziele – trägt die Verantwortung für dieses Ergebnis.« Schuster fürchtet weitreichende Folgen durch eine mögliche AfD-geführte Landesregierung, etwa durch eine radikal andere Bildungspolitik. »Der Schaden, den die sogenannte Alternative für Deutschland jetzt anrichten würde, wenn sie in Verantwortung gelangt, ist immens«, sagte er.

articles.title: Dänemark: Altkönigin Margrethe II. erneut in Krankenhaus eingeliefert
articles.excerpt: Dänemarks Altkönigin Margrethe II. ist seit diesem Sonntag im Krankenhaus. Die 86-Jährige wird wegen eines Blutergusses im Hüftbereich sowie leichter Dehydrierung behandelt, wie die Nachrichtenagentur Ritzau unter Berufung auf das Königshaus berichtete. Margrethe gehe es den Umständen entsprechend gut, sie sei guter Stimmung.Die ehemalige Königin wird den Angaben zufolge in der kommenden Woche zur Behandlung und Beobachtung im Krankenhaus bleiben – und deshalb auch die Beisetzung des norwegischen Königs Harald V. am Mittwoch in Oslo verpassen. Margrethe muss bereits zum dritten Mal in diesem Jahr im Krankenhaus behandelt werden.

articles.title: Grönland: Ursula Von der Leyen zu Besuch eingetroffen – Zeichen gegen Donald Trump
articles.excerpt: Ursula von der Leyen (rechts) mit Dänemarks Regierungschefin Mette Frederiksen und dem grönländischen Ministerpräsidenten Jens-Frederik Nielsen Foto: Mads Claus Rasmussen / Ritzau Scanpix / AP Ungeachtet der Kontrollansprüche von US-Präsident Donald Trump arbeitet die EU daran, ihre Zusammenarbeit mit Grönland zu stärken. Von der Leyen teilte zu ihrer Ankunft mit, es gehe darum, eine einzigartige Partnerschaft weiter zu festigen. »Wir sind Familie«, schrieb sie in sozialen Netzwerken.
